description.text: Tellus, also called Terra or Terra Mater, is the Roman personification of the Earth and the original earth goddess worshipped in the Republic and earlier periods.  The 1st‑century BC scholar Varro lists her among the twenty principal gods of Rome and one of the twelve agricultural deities, and she is closely associated with Ceres in rituals that celebrate earth and agricultural fertility.  Tellus is typically depicted reclining or rising waist‑high from a hole in the ground, holding a cornucopia or bunches of flowers, and her male counterpart is a sky god such as Caelus or a form of Jupiter.  Her Greek counterpart is Gaia, and the Etruscans called her Cel.  Scholars such as Michael Lipka argue that the Terra Mater who emerged during Augustus’ reign was a direct transfer of the Greek Ge Mater into Roman practice, while Tellus, whose temple lay within Rome’s sacred boundary, represents the original earth goddess cultivated by state priests.

The Temple of Tellus, the most prominent landmark of the fashionable Carinae neighborhood on the Oppian Hill, was originally vowed in 268 BC by Publius Sempronius Sophus after an earthquake during a battle with the Picenes.  The temple’s anniversary, celebrated on December 13, was marked by a lectisternium (banquet) for Ceres and by a festival of sow sacrifice during the Secular Games of 17 BC.  Tellus was also central to the Fordicidia, a festival instituted by Numa Pompilius in which a pregnant cow was sacrificed to assure the fertility of the grain already growing in the womb of Mother Earth.  In iconography, Tellus often appears as the central figure on the Italia relief panel of the Ara Pacis, surrounded by bucrania and motifs of vegetative and animal fertility, symbolizing the abundance of the earth.

curiosities.text: The Temple of Tellus was located on the Oppian Hill near the homes of Pompey and the Cicero family, making it a prominent landmark in a fashionable Roman neighborhood.
The Fordicidia festival, instituted by Numa Pompilius, required the sacrifice of a pregnant cow to placate Tellus and ensure the fertility of the earth’s crops.
Tellus is often depicted on the Italia relief panel of the Ara Pacis, where she is framed by bucrania and symbols of vegetative and animal fertility, underscoring her role as a source of abundance.
In Roman religious practice, Tellus was invoked at births and weddings, reflecting her status as a guardian of life and fertility.

The name Tellus is still used in modern Romance languages—such as Terra in Italian, Tierra in Spanish, and Terre in French—to refer to the planet Earth, and it occasionally appears in English as the adjective "tellurian."
